lawyer:
Dr. M Zahir, with M Hasan. Md. Firoz Shah and Md. Abdul Khair, Advocates -----For the petitioner 
Moinul Huq, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party Nos. 1 & 2.
parties:
Industrial Development Leasing Company of Bangladesh Ltd ----- Plaintiff-Petitioner
Vs
Reza Biscuit and Bread Co.Ltd. and others ----- Defendant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. Before the trial Court opposite-parties 1-4 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing written statement and their case is that they failed to install the machineries in time due to the fault of the erectors and gas supply. The Money Suit was ultimately decreed on contest by the trial Court by judgment dated 16.1.92 and the decree was drawn up on 16.2.92. Thereafter the decree was put into execution but at that time it came to the notice of the petitioner that instead of directing sale of the mortgaged 'Kha' schedule property by foreclosure the trial Court directed foreclosure of plaint Schedule 'Ka' property. The petitioner then by a petition moved the trial Court for amendment of the judgment and decree by incorporating 'Kha' schedule property in place of 'Ka' schedule property. The learned Subordinate Judge, thereafter, by order dated 23.11.1992 rejected the petition filed under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff-petitioner then moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 5. As against this Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submits that section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not contemplate such correction. The decree may be corrected if it is not in conformity with the judgment. Here, in this case the decree is in full conformity with the judgment If anything is to be done for variance of the judgment as submitted by Dr. Zahir, his remedy lies either in a petition for review of the judgment or in appeal. The trial Court cannot correct the judgment under the provision of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure as it is not a clerical or arithmetical mistake or mistake on omission. He argued that the trial Court consciously by its own hand incorporated the last portion of the sentence, that is, the foreclosure of the plaint 'Ka' schedule property. So, it cannot be found that this is a typing mistake. This portion of the ordering portion of the judgment was written by the Judge himself. So the correction of this, if any, must be by an appeal or a review petition but not under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If any error in the judgment is to be corrected it must be corrected either by an appeal or by review but not in the manner as prayed for by the plaintiff. 

 6. Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties lastly contends that the petition filed by the plaintiff for correction is barred by limitation as he had notice of the decree at least when he got the certified copy of the decree and put it into execution. Such petition for correction is not contemplated under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 "152. Clerical or arithmetical mistake in judgments, decrees or orders or errors arising therein from any accidental slip or omission may at any time be corrected by the Court either of its own motion or on the application of any of the parties". 

 8. So, from a perusal of this provision of section 152 of the Code it appears that any clerical or arithmetical mistake in judgment, decrees, or orders or errors arising therein, that is, in the judgments and decrees or orders or errors from any accidental slip or omission may be corrected by the Court at any time either of its own motion or on the application filed by an aggrieved party. 

 9. Dr. M. Zahir while arguing the case submits that the language of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure is wide enough to include any accidential slip or omission of which the source may be somewhere other than the judgment and decree. He submits that the machineries imported were leased out to the defendants on rental basis. That is the clear plaint case which has not been denied by the defendants. He also submits that 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged with the plaintiff by the defendants as a security for their advance which also has not been denied. When 'Ka' schedule property admittedly belonged to the plaintiff and leased out to the defendant on rental basis the decree cannot be satisfied by selling their own properties which very well indicate that the insertion of word 'Ka' in the ordering portion of the judgment is a mistake committed by the trial Court. He further submits that the question of foreclosure comes when a property is mortgaged and in this case 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged by the defendants. At our instance the parties placed the plaint and the written statement for our perusal. In Para 6 of the plaint it has been specifically stated as follows: 

 11. While arguing their cases the learned Advocates placed several decisions of the higher courts of the sub-continent in support of their respective cases. One such case which is very relevant in the matter was placed by Dr. Zahir which is reported in 22 DLR 130 (Province of East Pakistan Vs. His Highness Maharaja Kirit Bikram Kishore Deve Barman Manikya Bahadur), where a Division Bench of this Court has held that the language of section 152 is wide enough to include any accidential slip or omission of which the source may be somewhere other than the judgment and the decree. 

 13. Dr. Zahir also placed another decision though of the Single Bench of this Court reported in 29 DLR 81 (Ibrahim Sk. and others Vs. Janab Sk. alias Janab Ali Sk. & others), where it has been held that where a mistake has crept into the description of an item of property in the plaint schedule and the mistake has been carried over in the decree, the Court certainly has power to correct the error in the decree. It has also been held that if the court is satisfied that the mistake made by the parties in the pleadings is an accidental slip or omission or is due to inadvertence and it is so palpable that nobody can possibly have any doubt as to what the parties meant, the Court can set it right. The decision it appears has been based on the cases reported in 19 CWN 1021 (Mohabir Prosod Vs. Chandra Sekhar) and AIR 1952 Cal. 86 (Bela Deb; Vs. Bam Behari Roy). Dr. Zahir placing reliance on this decision contends that when there was a scope for making correction after passing the decree the mistake as noticed in the decree may very well be corrected by the trial Court. 

 14. Dr. Zahir also placed reliance in another decision reported in AIR (PC) 136 (MRKRM Somasudram Chetty Vs. MRMVL Subramanian Chetty), where it has been held that accidental slip or misstatement of the Judge's intention in the judgment can also be corrected. Dr. Zahir submits that the learned Judge ordered that the defendants should satisfy the decree within 60 days but in case of their failure the plaintiff company may get back their money through the process of the court by foreclosing the plaint schedule 'Ka' property. But the question of foreclosing of 'Ka' schedule property does not arise when 'Kha' schedule property was mortgaged. So this is an accidental slip or misstatement of trial Judge's intention which is liable to correction. 

 15. Dr. Zahir also placed reliance in another decision reported in AIR 1967 (SC) 1440 (Samarendra Nath Singha and another Vs. Krishna Kumar Nag), where it has been held that errors arising from accidental slip can be corrected subsequently not only in the decree drawn up by ministerial officer but even in the judgment pronounced and signed by the Court. From this also Dr. Zahir submits that mistake committed by the trial Court is very much apparent as for realisation of the decretal dues the trial Court cannot order for foreclosure of 'Ka' schedule property which admittedly belongs to the plaintiff decree-holder. 

 "As to the observation of the High Court Division that the disputed figures in the judgment were put deliberately by the trial Court, we do not find any basis for this observation in that it is the trial Court which replaced item No. 131 by item No. 132 and the figures 154 by the figures 134 without any basis whatever. This mistake or error is found to have been caused by accidential slip, and correction thereof is within the scope and ambit of section 152 of Civil Procedure Code. For correction of such mistake no separate suit is contemplated in the Civil Procedure Code". 

 17. Placing reliance on this decision Dr. Zahir submits that it is nobody's case that 'Ka' schedule property was mortgaged, rather it is the admitted case that 'Kha' schedule property has been mortgaged with the plaintiff. So, for foreclosure there cannot be any order for 'Ka' schedule property. So, this inclusion of 'Ka' schedule property in the ordering portion of the judgment is an accidental slip and this may be corrected under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Dr. Zahir placing the judgment of the trial Court submits that the trial Court came to the finding that the plaintiff company has succeeded in proving their case and as such the company is entitled to get the relief prayed for and thereafter the court ordered that the decree be passed accordingly. For proper appreciation let us quote here the ordering portion of the judgment and it runs as follows: 

 "that the suit be decreed on contest against the defendant Nos. 1-4 with costs. The defendant Nos. 1-4 are hereby jointly and severally directed to pay a sum of Taka 1,40,52,942.00 only + costs of the suit to the plaintiff company within 60 (sixty) days from this day, failing which, the plaintiff company will be entitled to realise the said amount along with the costs of the suit through the process of the court by foreclosing the plaint schedule 'Ka' property". 

 19. As against this Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 submits that such a mistake, if any, may be corrected only by an appeal preferred against the judgment and decree or by a petition for review of the judgment. The provision of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure has no manner of application. He submits that if the decree drawn up is not in conformity with the judgment this may be corrected under section 152 of the' Code of Civil Procedure, but if the judgment is to be corrected it is by way of review or appeal. Placing a Single Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in AIR 1953 (Cal) 257 (Nirmal Chakrabarti and others Vs. Land Acquisition Collector, Alipur and others) Mr. Huq contends that the mistake as submitted by the petitioner is not a clerical or arithmetical mistake or accidental slip or omission. Considering the facts and circumstances of that case it was held that amendments sought for does not come within the ambit of mistake or accidental slip referred to in section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that decision it has been held that section 152 of the Code deals only with correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes, or accidental slips or omissions. The nature of the amendment concerned cannot by any stretch of imagination be said to fall within the mistakes or slips as referred to in section 152 of the Code. Mr. Huq contends that in the present case the trial Judge deliberately wrote 'Ka' schedule property instead of 'Kha’ schedule property and that was done consciously which was incorporated by his own hand and there is no scope for correction. This inclusion of 'Ka" schedule property is deliberate. So, no relief is available to the plaintiff-petitioner under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 "10. In the facts of the case the plaintiff pointed out the error which needed rectification and that could be done only by way of review. The error crept in the ordering portion while prescribing the mode of payment without assigning any reason thereof in the body of the judgment. Where nothing was said in the judgment about it, the Court, however, in the decree laid down a mode of payment which was not the bargain of the parties. Thus clearly a case of review was made out and it was incumbent upon the Courts below to allow the review because its variation was neither set up by the parties nor the variation in mode of payment flowed from the judgment, so as to reflect in the decree which is mode of formal expression of the adjudication made by the Court. The Privy Council says, it is imperative that it should conform to the judgment. (Ord. 20, rule 6). Every Court has power to amend its decree so as to carry out its own meaning (section 152). For the purpose of interpreting a decree no other document is so directly in point as the judgment or can in the nature of things, have comparable force "Manakchand Vs. Monoarlal, AIR 1944 PC 46". 

 22. The learned Advocate contends that the alleged mistake pointed out by the petitioner can only be rectified or corrected by review of the judgment or in an appeal and section 152 of the Code is not applicable for such correction or rectification. 

 23. Mr. Huq also placed reliance in another decision reported in 23 DLR, 45 (Tejendra Chandra Dhar and others Vs. Rohini Ranjan Saha and another), where it has been held that a decree may be corrected only under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure if it is not in conformity with the judgment. 

 24. Mr. Huq lastly placed reliance in the decision reported in 4 DLR (PC) 1 (Piyaratana Unnase Vs. Wahareka Sounuttara Unnase), where it has been held that the Court may at any time either of its own motion or on the application filed by any or the aggrieved parties correct any clerical or arithmetical mistake of the judgment or order arising therein from any accidental slip or omission which is necessary to bring the decree into conformity with the judgment. It has been held that the general rule is clear that once an order is passed and entered or otherwise perfected, in accordance with the practice of the Court, the court which passed the order is "funcus officio" and cannot set aside or alter the order however wrong it may appear to be. That can only be done on appeal. The learned Advocate contends that the trial Court in the present case intentionally included 'Ka' schedule property in the ordering portion of the judgment which finds place in the decree itself. There is no clerical or arithmetical mistake or omission or slip as emphasised under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. So, the trial court rightly rejected the plaintiff's prayer for amendment of the judgment. 

 25. We have carefully heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and also gone through the decisions cited by them in support of their respective contentious. The consistent view of the higher courts of this sub-continent including the Privy Council is that the decree may be amended if it is not in conformity with the judgment. This is the consistent view and there is no doubt about it. The decree should reflect what has been stated in the judgment and if the decree does not reflect that, it may be corrected under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But here in the present case before us the petitioner's contention is not on wrong drawing up of the decree but their case is that the trial Court committed an accidental slip or omission in incorporating 'Ka' schedule property instead of 'Kha' schedule property in the ordering portion of the judgment. We have carefully gone through the plaint, written statement and judgment and it appears that the definite case of the plaintiff is that 'Ka' schedule property was leased out on rental basis to the defendant and 'Kha' schedule property was duly mortgaged by the defendants in favour of the plaintiff which was necessary for security of their loan or advance. 

 26. The trial Court after examination of the evidence adduced from the side of the parties came to the clear finding that the plaintiff is entitled to the decree prayed for and passed the necessary order but while writing the ordering portion the trial Court directed that in case of failure of the defendants to pay the decretal amount to the plaintiff company within 60 days from the date of the judgment, the plaintiff company will be at liberty to realise the decretal amount along with the costs of the suit through process of the Court by foreclosing the plaint schedule 'Ka' property. 

 28. Mr. Moinul Huq cited certain decisions which we have incorporated above, where it has been decided that a decree may be corrected if it is not in conformity with the judgment. There is no dispute on the proposition of law but it is not the case before us. The case before us is that the ordering portion of the judgment was not drawn up in accordance with the contents of the judgment. The petitioner's prayer is for the correction of the ordering portion of the judgment which is not in accordance with the pleadings of the parties as well as of the contents of the body of judgment. The mistake is only in the ordering portion. So the decisions cited by Mr Huq has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case before us. So we are of the view that for this small omission or accidental slip the plaintiff cannot be forced to prefer an appeal or file a review petition. 

 29. Mr. Huq also raised a plea of limitation and he submits that the decree was, drawn up in accordance with the terms of the judgment with notice to the plaintiff and the plaintiff took the certified copy of the decree and put it into execution and when they were proceeding with the execution the so-called defect came to their notice and thereafter they filed a petition for correction of the judgment. But by this time a long period has elapsed. He argued that such a petition under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure ought to have been filed within the shortest possible time and on the obtaining of the certified copy of the judgment with the so-called wrong contents. But it has been held in the decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 125 (Ismail ullah being dead his heirs Baizid Vila and others Vs. Sukumar Chandra Das and others that the decree may be amended at any time, of course if it is not in conformity with the judgment. Quoting from the decision of the case of MRKRM Somasundram Chetty Vs. MRMVL Subramaniah Chetty reported in AIR 1926 (PC) 136 the Appellate Division opined that the decree may be amended. In that decision of the Privy Council it has been decided as follows: 

 "It is, however, urged that section 152 gives the Court a discretion to allow or not an application for amendment of a decree. In my opinion, this is not the correct reading of the section. It no doubt says that when a clerical or arithmetical mistake is discovered in the decree, the Court may at any time correct it. The word 'may' in the section does not make it discretionary with the Court to order the correction but merely enlarges the power of the Court by providing that such correction can be done "at any time" or in other words, the section simply emphasises that no lapse of time would disentitle the court to make the correction. As has been observed, the intention of the law is to make it obligatory upon the Court whenever any such mistake is discovered to correct it and section 152 merely emphasises that duty of the Court by saying that it may be done at any time without limitation." 

 34. The decree should also be corrected accordingly. 

 The execution case shall proceed after making necessary correction in the judgment and decree. The petitioner should produce a fresh certified copy of the decree before the executing court after its correction.
